source.title: Can We Trust AI in 6G? Verifiable and Auditable AI-Driven Trustworthy Wireless Networks
source.authors: Genze Jiang; Yi-Zhou Huang; Ke-Zhi Wang

page_placements.theme: SAE and dictionary features as causal control units (not neurons)

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses sparse-autoencoder features to build and evaluate a mechanistic auditing method for LTE signalling. It does not test whether neuron poles have one main job or test any other listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The study measures and intervenes on sparse-autoencoder features, not neuron poles. Its feature-alignment and ablation findings bear on the general use of internal features as analysis units, so they are recorded with versions ["none"]. It does not test the neuron-pole shares, cross-model/scale shares, Inception examples, attribution graphs, explanation prediction, or automated explanation scores in V1–V7. The paper also cites results from other work, which are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study builds an auditing method on sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features in a LoRA-adapted Qwen3-0.6B for LTE signalling. It does not measure neuron poles, neuron-explanation shares, InceptionV1 neurons, neuron-based attribution graphs or simulation scores. It neither tests nor relies on the neurons-already-clean finding. It mentions the topic only by citing prior work that SAE features 'tend to be more interpretable than individual neurons', with no result of its own on neurons. So T6 rather than the reader's T4: it uses SAEs as a tool, not the claim's finding.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors propose mechanistic auditing: locate protocol-aligned SAE features, verify their causal role by removal against random and concept-selective controls, then audit each decision. In the case study, removing handover features lowers handover accuracy from 96% to 0%, while random features of equal number change it by under 2 points. They name evaluation on live-network agents as the next step.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses sparse-autoencoder features aligned to executable 3GPP predicates, then tests feature dependence by removal. It does not score neuron poles for one-job explanations or test explanations against new activating examples.
record.method_sensitivity: The relative effect of aligned versus random feature removal changes with depth: the reported loss ratio is about 2.4 at the first layer and about four and a half at the last layer.

fits_no_version.finding: In LoRA-adapted Qwen3-0.6B, removing concept-aligned SAE features drops held-out accuracy from 59.2% to 4.2%, against 46.8% for random features at the last layer. Removing the 58 handover features drops handover-task accuracy from 96% to 0%, versus an 8.5-point loss on other tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features aligned to executable 3GPP protocol predicates have large, concept-selective causal effects on an LTE-signalling model's decisions.

fits_no_version.finding: Across eight language models, 45–52% of SAE features align with at least one protocol concept, including two models scoring under 10% on the tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The proportion of SAE features aligned with domain concepts is roughly stable across models and does not track task competence.

record.problems: The case study uses one fixed-seed run; the paper does not report uncertainty intervals. It evaluates recorded LTE signalling tasks rather than live closed-loop network control, and the authors say the autoencoder's faithfulness and the cost of real-platform gating remain open issues.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. The adapted model's standalone held-out accuracy and cited findings from other studies were not entered as results about internal analysis units.

untested.parts: All: the Qwen3-32B neuron-pole shares (one job, two jobs, not understood) are not measured; only SAE features in Qwen3-0.6B.
All: no neuron-share measures across models or scale. The 45–52% figure is an SAE feature-alignment proportion to 15 protocol concepts.
All: no vision models, InceptionV1 neurons or recursive-generalization analysis.
All: no comparison of architectures, regularization or tools on neuron interpretability.
All: no attribution graphs from neurons and no comparison with replacement models.
All: no test of whether explanations from activating examples predict neuron firing.
All: no simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The analysis unit is SAE features, not neurons. The paper's one remark on neurons is a cited claim (Huben et al.) that SAE features are more interpretable than neurons, not a result. Single fixed-seed run with no uncertainty reported; the eight-model comparison is reported only in aggregate. All rows correctly link to 'none'.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole shares and the one-job, two-job, and not-understood categories.
Neuron-pole shares across models, architectures, and scale.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, and recursive generalization.
Architecture, regularization, and tool effects on neuron interpretability, including the vision-model estimates.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and their reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fit activating examples but fail to predict activations on new examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.
